title: The quest to keep organs alive outside the body
gist: A Checkup newsletter survey of the organ-preservation field: supercooling pig kidneys to -4 °C for days (Powell Palm, no cryoprotectants), cryopreservation that works routinely for eggs/sperm/embryos at -196 °C but has never worked for a whole human organ, cryonics at Alcor as a distinct and unproven bet, and machine perfusion that now sustains livers and kidneys ~24 hours and is being extended to eyeballs and uteruses. The framing thesis is the organ bank — stores of organs preserved long enough to test, match, and ship.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on donor organ supply is time, not only donor numbers — organs survive only hours outside the body even on ice, which is why doctors want organ banks that hold organs for days, weeks or longer.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Reframes the shortage as a logistics/storage problem with a technology fix, rather than a donor-recruitment problem — that is where the venture capital should go.
insights.locator: There's a huge shortage of donor organs

insights.claim: Long-duration organ storage would unlock three separate capabilities at once: running tests on organs before use, finding the best recipient matches, and transporting organs to those recipients.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Each capability is a separate revenue surface — diagnostics on banked organs, matching software, and cold-chain logistics — not just one product.

insights.claim: One team has supercooled pig kidneys — animals whose organs are similar in size to human ones — kept them at -4 °C for days, and successfully reimplanted them, a result described as a landmark achievement.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Pig-scale organs are the accepted proxy for human organs, so this is a directly translatable result rather than a small-animal curiosity.
insights.locator: In new research, one team has been able to supercool the kidneys of pigs

insights.claim: Matthew Powell Palm's supercooling approach outperformed ice storage without requiring cryoprotectants, while other teams are still pursuing chemical cocktails to reach lower temperatures and longer storage.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Two distinct technical bets are running in parallel — chemical-free/shorter-duration versus chemical/longer-duration; the regulatory clock favours the chemical-free one.
insights.locator: Powell Palm is working on other ways to preserve organs

insights.claim: Ice formation is a binary failure mode in organ preservation — once ice forms, the crystals cause damage that renders the organ unusable — which is why the whole field is organised around avoiding nucleation rather than tolerating it.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Explains why incremental cooling gains are hard-won and why an ice-nucleation-control device is the defensible piece of IP.
insights.quote: Once ice forms in them, they’re done.
insights.locator: It has proved super difficult to freeze organs

insights.claim: Cryopreservation is routine for eggs, sperm and embryos — cooled to -196 °C in under two seconds and usable after decades in storage — yet no one has ever cryopreserved and thawed a human organ for transplantation.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The gap between cell-scale and organ-scale cryo is the key technical discontinuity — do not extrapolate IVF-industry success into organ banking timelines.

insights.claim: Gerontologist Stephen L. Coles' brain was perfused with cryoprotectants and cooled to -146 °C at Alcor in Arizona after his 2014 death, and cryobiologist Greg Fahy later found the shrunken brain cells bounced back on rewarming — which still does not mean the cells are alive or the brain could be reanimated.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Cryonics results are frequently mis-sold as evidence for organ banking; the cell-morphology-versus-viability distinction is the tell to test any such claim against.
insights.quote: There are so many ways those neurons could be toast.
insights.locator: In March, I wrote about Stephen L. Coles

insights.claim: Machine perfusion devices, which feed an organ nutrients to mimic body conditions, have become commonly used over the last decade and typically maintain livers and kidneys for up to about 24 hours.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: This is the installed-base incumbent any supercooling entrant has to displace or complement — its 24-hour ceiling is the benchmark to beat.
insights.locator: Another way to prolong the lifespan of an organ

insights.claim: Perfusion protocols are being adapted to a widening list of organs including eyeballs — a recent feat that could enable whole-eye transplants — and uteruses, with a Valencia team keeping a human uterus alive for a day on a system nicknamed “Mother.”
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Each newly perfusable organ opens a previously non-existent transplant market; watch eye and uterus perfusion as the next categories to commercialise.
insights.locator: Researchers are now adapting this protocol for a growing list of organs

insights.claim: The organ preservation field is described as positively buzzing with more MIT Technology Review coverage promised in coming weeks, signalling a cluster of results arriving rather than one isolated breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Clustered news flow is often the precursor to a funding cycle in a niche — worth positioning ahead of the coverage wave.
insights.quote: It’s an exciting time for organ preservation.
insights.locator: In March, I went to visit scientists in Valencia
